title: Hidden treasure (76–81)
hook: follow the one who points out your faults as if showing buried treasure; a solid rock is not shaken by wind

segments.voice: Yesterday, milk that turns slowly, and your line: it turns slowly. What slow consequence did you trace back? Day one hundred seventy-four, and chapter six: the wise.
screen: `MILK THAT TURNS SLOWLY — IT TURNS SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time someone told you something you didn't want to hear. Your boss said the report missed the point. A friend said you'd been short with them lately. Your kid said, “you're on your phone again.” What happened in your body? For most of us: heat in the face, a quick defense ready on the tongue, maybe a small list of their faults, just in case. Now imagine treating that moment the way you'd treat someone handing you a map to buried gold. That's how the sixth chapter of the Dhammapada begins. Today, verses seventy-six to eighty-one: hidden treasure.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU DIDN'T WANT TO HEAR.` → `HEAT IN THE FACE.` → `A MAP TO BURIED GOLD.`

segments.voice: Chapter six is called pandita, the wise one. You know the word already: English borrowed it, by way of Hindi, as pundit. Verse seventy-six says: if you find a wise person who points out your faults and corrects you, follow them as you'd follow someone who shows you hidden treasure. It will go better for you, not worse. The commentary tells it about an old man named Radha, so poor that the monks weren't sure he should be ordained. Sariputta, one of the Buddha's chief disciples, remembered that Radha had once given him a single spoonful of food, and took him on. Radha turned out to be the easiest student in the monastery. Every correction, he took gladly, and he thrived. Verse seventy-seven adds that the wise should admonish and hold others back from harm; the good will love them for it, only the bad won't. Then verse eighty, a lovely picture of craftsmen: “Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.” And verse eighty-one: “As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.” Put the two together. Correction is treasure. And blame and praise are both just wind. The wise person doesn't need praise to feel steady, and doesn't collapse under blame. They listen for what's useful, like Radha, and let the rest blow past. That's why the rock doesn't shake. Not because nothing hits it. Because it's rooted deeper than the weather.
screen: `PANDITA — THE WISE ONE.` · `CORRECTION AS BURIED TREASURE.` · `RADHA, THE EASIEST STUDENT.` · `BLAME AND PRAISE ARE BOTH WIND.` · then, large: `THE ROCK DOESN'T SHAKE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone who once corrected you, and was right. A teacher, a parent, a coach, a friend who said the hard thing. Remember the sting of it. Then remember what it gave you, what you learned or changed because of it. Let a little gratitude come, if it wants to. Then feel yourself as a rock: heavy, grounded, breathing. Let a word of praise drift by in your mind, and a word of blame. Both are wind. The rock doesn't shake. The bell holds the time.
Pandita. The wise one, who treats correction like treasure, fashions themselves like a craftsman, and stands like a rock in blame and praise.
Your line: the rock doesn't shake. Today, thank someone who corrected you, a message or a word. Tell them what it gave you. Day one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic life, being 'easy to admonish' is counted a virtue, and monks formally invite correction from one another, as at the end of the rains retreat.

fork.setup: you're Sariputta. a very poor old man wants to become a monk, and the others hesitate. you remember he once gave you a single spoonful of food. what do you do?
options: say nothing; it was only a spoonful.
take him on as your student.
give him food and send him home.
fork.reveal: Sariputta remembered the gift and took him on. Radha became the easiest student in the monastery.

original.note: Pali: wise one, learned one, the title of chapter six; English 'pundit' comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pandit is an expert who tells others what to think.
what it means: in the Dhammapada, the wise one welcomes correction and stays steady in blame and praise.
what a scholar hears: verse 76 calls the one who reproves you 'nidhinam va pavattaram,' like one who reveals treasures; the commentary ties it to Radha and Sariputta.
